title: Define accepted requests and responses
why: An API is the interface software uses to request work from other software. Its contract states allowed inputs, outputs and failures so callers can handle them.
dataset: The engineer prepares fictional request q-17: division=Retail, question=Can I pause for 10 days?, product absent. Compare product=Everyday with product supplied as an empty string.
metric: The test engineer checks that an absent product returns outcome=clarify, missing=[product] and retrievalCalls=0, meaning no search ran. An empty supplied product is invalid, not a known product.
evidence: Save q-17 and the response “Which Retail product: Everyday or Plus?” with retrievalCalls=0. Keep separate tests for absent, empty and permitted products; an assertion is a check that fails if the result differs.
decision: Which requesting applications and customer organisations may read or change each resource?

title: Record which source supports the answer
why: Source provenance means where information came from and which version may be used. Search and model training can carry forward errors or use information without permission.
dataset: The source owner supplies this fictional manifest, a record of approved source versions: applicableRevision=RE-7. RE-7 allows maximum=30 days subject to adviser eligibility confirmation. RE-8 allows maximum=45 days and state=draft. Ask: “What is the maximum pause?”
metric: The reviewer expects a citation to RE-7 and maximum 30 days subject to adviser eligibility confirmation. Any answer based on draft RE-8 fails because it is not the applicable approved source.
evidence: The engineer saves the manifest revision, source identifiers and answer with its source passage. Test withdrawing RE-7: its searchable passages and cached answers, which are saved previous results, must stop being eligible for use.
decision: Which data may leave the agreed environment, and how will withdrawn sources and retained data be removed?

title: Prepare reviewed cases for source search
why: Retrieval means finding relevant source passages. A golden dataset is a versioned set of questions with reviewed expected results, used to test whether search finds the evidence an answer needs.
dataset: The subject expert labels this fictional question: “Can an account under review take a pause?” Relevant passages are P1 (one pause per 12 months) and P2 (accounts under review excluded). Search returns P1 and unrelated fee passage P9 as its top two results.
metric: The test engineer calculates recall@2 = 1/2 = 50%: one of the two relevant passages appears in the top two results. Hit@2 = 1 means at least one relevant passage was found. Missing P2 still prevents an answer to the exclusion question.
evidence: Save the source collection version, reviewed relevant IDs [P1,P2] and returned order [P1,P9]. The subject expert requires the exclusion P2 before the answer can settle eligibility; finding P1 alone does not grant permission.
decision: Which source passages are necessary to settle each question, and who reviews that expectation?

title: Check that each answer claim follows from its source
why: Grounding means supporting an answer with the source evidence. A convincing sentence and a real citation can still make a claim that the source does not support.
dataset: The reviewer receives fictional source EX-2: a specialist may review a 45-day request. Question: “Will a 45-day pause be approved?” Candidate answer: “Your 45-day pause will be approved [EX-2].”
metric: The reviewer marks the approval claim unsupported because permission to review does not guarantee approval. Expected correction: “A specialist may review a 45-day request, but EX-2 does not guarantee approval.”
evidence: The test engineer saves the candidate, exact EX-2 passage, reviewer’s unsupported-claim label and correction. The check must reject the approval promise even though its citation identifies a real source.
decision: Which unsupported promise could harm a user, and who decides the acceptable response?

title: Test actions and who may authorise them
why: A tool is an operation an agent or application can call, such as creating a purchase. The receiving service must check permission because a request can change real records.
dataset: The test engineer supplies fictional purchase amount=1200, requesterRole=team-lead, reason=Urgent replacement, approveException=true. Rule P1 sends amounts above 1000 to Finance; only Finance may approve exceptions.
metric: Check route=Finance, exceptionApproved=false and submittedPurchases=0. The request’s approveException flag is supplied data; it does not grant the requester Finance authority.
evidence: Save the input, verified signed-in role, permission decision and check of the stored purchase count. For a separate retry case, two identical submissions with request key ref-31 must return referral R-8 and create only one referral.
decision: Which actions need a person’s approval, who may give it, and which exact action details do they approve?

title: Check automated scorers against reviewed answers
why: An automated evaluator, or judge, assigns quality labels or scores. Calibration checks its decisions against independently reviewed human labels before anyone relies on its scores.
dataset: The policy specialist supplies fictional reviewed labels: referral-required=Q1–Q5; routine=Q6–Q10. The judge predicts referral for Q1,Q2,Q3,Q6 and routine for the other six.
metric: The test engineer counts TP=3 (correct referrals), FP=1 (unnecessary referral), FN=2 (missed referrals), TN=4 (correct routine cases). Referral precision=3/4=75% is correct referrals divided by predicted referrals; recall=3/5=60% is referrals found divided by referrals needed; false-positive rate=1/5=20% is unnecessary referrals divided by routine cases.
evidence: Save the rubric version, meaning the scoring rules, and all ten human/judge label pairs. The policy specialist reviews Q4 and Q5 (missed referrals) and Q6 (false referral); unresolved disagreement remains visible before judge scores inform a decision.
decision: Who reviews disagreements, and which judge errors prevent its scores being used?

title: Compare changes and acknowledge uncertainty
why: A higher score on a sample may occur by chance. Compare both versions on the same cases and estimate how uncertain the difference is before deciding.
dataset: The test engineer records fictional paired results on the same 100 cases: both pass=74, only A passes=6, only B passes=10, both fail=10. Each case is the comparison unit; repeated calls for it are not new independent cases.
metric: A succeeds on 80/100; B on 84/100. Paired gain=(10−6)/100=4 percentage points. This estimated gain is below the predeclared 5-point practical-gain target, the improvement the team agreed would matter.
evidence: Save each case’s A and B results, the practical-gain rule and an uncertainty calculation that keeps each pair together. The decision owner must not call B a demonstrated improvement from the two totals alone.
decision: What improvement would justify a change, and what would it cost to declare a winner that is not actually better?

title: Check whether the live service is useful and timely
why: Operations means the work of running and supporting a live service. A fast response is not a successful outcome when it is wrong or unusable.
dataset: The service owner reviews fictional ten eligible requests: seven correct answers within five seconds; one correct referral in four seconds; one error page in one second; one correct answer in eight seconds.
metric: The test engineer counts useful-and-timely outcomes=(7+1)/10=80%, below a proposed 90% target. Nine fast responses include the error page, so they do not equal nine useful outcomes.
evidence: Save request identifiers, result codes, elapsed time and review labels without message text. Separately, one confirmed disclosure between customer organisations triggers private-source search shutdown and the assigned incident responder’s action.
decision: Which failure requires stopping or restoring the service, and what may its monitoring records retain?

title: Check that the model can serve the planned workload
why: Model serving runs a model to answer requests. Fitting it in memory is not enough: it must also respond promptly and meet the task-quality requirement under the planned load.
dataset: The hosting engineer prepares an illustrative load run: 100 prompts, each 1000 input tokens and capped at 100 output tokens, at concurrency 10. Tokens are pieces of text counted by the model; concurrency is requests in progress together. A and B use the same reviewed cases.
metric: The proposed p95 first-token limit=2 seconds measures the time until output starts for the 95th percentile of requests. Illustrative fixture A=1.8 seconds, B=3.2 seconds: B fails this workload’s delay limit. Task-quality results must pass separately.
evidence: Save hardware and model versions, run settings, timing for every request, output lengths and quality labels. The hosting engineer hands these to the service owner. These fictional timings illustrate a decision; they are not provider benchmarks.
decision: Do lower-precision model weights (quantization) or processing requests together (batching) retain quality while meeting the service target?

title: Keep final comparison cases out of development
why: Adaptation changes prompts or model parameters to improve performance. A holdout is data kept out of that work so the final comparison does not reward familiarity with the test.
dataset: The test engineer checks fictional advisory cases: A1 and A2 share one client source; B1 and C1 are unrelated. Proposed development=[A1,B1], held-out=[A2,C1]. Jo has read A1 while editing the prompt.
metric: The split fails because A2 shares the source already exposed to development. Use development=[A1,A2,B1] and held-out=[C1]. Jo must not inspect C1 while editing the prompt.
evidence: Save source-group identifiers, the split manifest (which case belongs in which group) and who has seen each group. If C1 is used to improve the prompt, mark it exposed and collect a new independent comparison set.
decision: What evidence would show that prompt changes or training improve on the simpler starting approach?

title: Review generated cases before treating them as evidence
why: Synthetic data means examples produced by a generator rather than independently collected from the work. Many generated variations can repeat the same wrong assumption.
dataset: The reviewer inspects a fictional generator’s 20 variants of G-12, all labelled answer-yes because 20+10=30. RE-7 permits only one pause per 12 months; G-12’s earlier pause was four months ago.
metric: The policy owner rejects all 20 labels: the reviewed result is referral-required, with no approval promise. Twenty rewordings of the same wrong answer do not test independent policy situations.
evidence: Save the generator version, original case G-12, rejected labels and correction reason. The test engineer keeps all variants with G-12 in the exposed regression group, used to recheck known failures. Collect separate unseen cases for final comparison.
decision: Which real situations are absent from the generated cases, and who will supply independent examples?
